set.rappels: Over the top by the standard Colchuck Balanced Rock descent: one rappel of about 30 m east off a slung horn on the summit block, then scree clockwise around the peak. Retreat from the lower half has no documented single-rope line: the bolted Sky Lounge anchors lead to two rappels of about 40 m, which one 60 m rope does not reach.
set.descent_text: After topping out via Let it Burn’s upper pitches, take the standard summit descent: an optional single rappel of about 30 m from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak back to the base. To retreat from the lower half instead, rappel to the Sky Lounge, the two-bolt ledge atop pitch 3, stopping first at the Kerwin’s Crack anchor if your rope does not reach it in one; from the Sky Lounge, the way back to the approach gully is two rappels of about 40 m each. A single 60 m rope reaches only about 30 m per rappel, so those stations are beyond one rope and no intermediate station is known.

review.single_rope: Summit descent is one ~30 m rappel (fits a 60 m rope, optional) plus a scree scramble. The lower-half retreat is two ~40 m rappels; no source gives a single-rope alternative.
review.changed: Removed the 80 m / two-rope wording; stated plainly that the 40 m retreat rappels exceed one 60 m rope. Kept the existing one-station table (30 m).

set.rappels: 3 rappels on a single 60 m rope down the line of ascent, from chains on the summit, a bolted chain anchor and a tree or bush at the pitch-1 ledge
set.rappel_count_note: Three rappels on one 60 m rope is the standard North Face descent and is what these stations describe. The claim that the whole line is bolts and chains with no natural gear required is not accurate: the last station, on the pitch-1 ledge, is webbing on a tree or a small bush, so carry webbing and a ring. Keep this distinct from the South Face descent used when linking Concord with Lexington — that is a separate two-rappel line of roughly 30 m each with its own bolted mid-face station, and its stations must not be mixed with these.

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel from the summit down the upper North Face.
rappel_detail.anchor: summit double-bolt chains (a small tree is also reported at the top anchor)
hazards: The move from the summit onto the anchor is short but exposed and clumsy in boots or with a pack on.
This face stays wet after rain and can be icy early and late in the season, and the rappel stances are where that is felt.
rappel_detail.station: Rap chains on the summit, reached from the true summit by a short, awkward step and slither over the top of the summit block; a small tree is reported beside the top anchor as well.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge atop pitch 1.
hazards: The landing ledge is vegetated and the brush catches rope ends on both the throw and the pull.
Slab above the station stays greasy after rain.
rappel_detail.station: Bolted chain anchor on the climbing line just below the 5.0 slab section of pitch 3. The rappel from it drops to the bushy, tree-dotted ledge at the top of pitch 1.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull well out from the notch so the strands come down clear of the brush on the ledge above.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel from the ledge back to the base of the climb at the notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree or bush with webbing, not fixed hardware
hazards: A tree or bush anchor rather than fixed hardware — this is the one station on the descent where you may have to build or replace, so carry webbing and a rap ring.
The rappel lands at the notch, which is the top of the loose approach gully every party climbing Liberty Bell and Concord walks up. Anything dislodged goes straight down it.
rappel_detail.station: The station on the bushy pitch-1 ledge, from which the last rappel returns you to the base of the climb at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Do not plan on this one being fixed hardware: parties on the ground have rappelled off webbing on the tree here, and another party's anchor at this level was a small bush that held under testing but was plainly not bomber.

review.single_rope: Three rappels on one 60 m rope: two on chains, the last off webbing on a tree at the pitch-1 ledge. Single-rope is the usual way; ropes can stick in cracks on pulls.
review.changed: Removed the asides about combining the top two rappels on a second rope; kept stations, lengths and hazards. descent_text already single-rope, left unchanged.

set.rappels: 2 rappels of about 30 m on a single 60 m rope down the south face from the summit chains to the Concord-Lexington notch, the second from a bolted mid-face station. The north face also goes, in three stages, but ropes tend to stick there.

review.single_rope: South face: two ~30 m rappels on one 60 m rope with a bolted mid-face station; the first is a full 30 m so the rope's middle mark must be centred. North face: three stages.
review.changed: Removed the parenthetical about a second rope in the summary. Table already valid single-rope (30 m stations); descent_text already single-rope.

set.rappels: 2 rappels of about 30 m on a single 60 m rope down the south face to the Concord-Lexington notch, the second from a bolted mid-face station
set.descent_text: Downclimb, or rappel with a single 60 m rope in two stages of about 30 m, using the bolted intermediate station partway down the south face.

review.single_rope: Two ~30 m rappels on one 60 m rope with chains midway down the face; first rappel is a full 30 m, so centre the rope.
review.changed: Removed the second-rope aside from the summary and the full-length single-rappel sentence from descent_text. Table kept (valid single-rope).

set.rappels: 2 rappels on a single 60 m rope from the south side of the summit
set.rappel_count_note: Two rappels on one 60 m rope is the standard count. Individual station lengths are not documented, though the first is a full-length pull of about 30 m, so centre the rope.
set.descent_text: Downclimb, or rappel with a single 60 m rope in two shorter stages off the intermediate anchor station near the corners.

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel from the summit to an intermediate anchor station near the corners, on a single 60 m rope.
Second rappel from the intermediate station down to the notch; carry a spare rappel device.
rappel_detail.anchor: intermediate anchor station near the corners

review.single_rope: South face of Concord goes in two ~30 m rappels on one 60 m rope via the mid-face chains.
review.changed: Removed the full-length single-rappel alternative from the note, table note and descent_text.

set.rappels: 3 rappels on a single 60 m rope: two down the summit’s west side, breaking at the mid-height station, then one down pitch 1’s north face to the notch
set.rappel_count_note: The mid-height station is reported by only one source and its condition is unconfirmed; check it before relying on it.
set.descent_text: Rappel off the summit's west side, stopping at the mid-height station, to a ledge; move right along it and make one more rappel down the north face to the notch.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of 3 on a single 60 m rope, to the mid-height station.
rappel_detail.station: The summit, on the west side.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of 3, to a ledge. Move right along the ledge.
rappel_detail.station: The mid-height station on the west side.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of 3, down pitch 1’s north face to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.
rappel_detail.anchor: anchor on the ledge above pitch 1
rappel_detail.station: The ledge, after moving right along it.

review.single_rope: One report saw an anchor partway down the first west-side rappel, suggesting one rope works in two steps; no source gives lengths or confirms the anchor's condition.
review.changed: Removed the second-rope asides from the summary, table note and descent_text; added a caution that the mid-height station is thinly documented.

set.rappels: No single-rope descent is documented. The one recorded descent used one rappel at the headwall crack, then a long and a short rappel from the north-ridge horn at lengths a single 60 m rope may not match; the route has also been downclimbed with no rappels on a low-angle southeast wall that bypasses the summit cliffs.
set.rappel_count_note: The one recorded descent made three rappels — one at the headwall crack, then a long one and a short one from the north-ridge horn. Only the headwall rappel is known to suit a single strand of a 30-40 m rope. The horn rappels were longer than one 60 m rope reaches (about 30 m), and no intermediate station is known, so what one rope does there is not documented. The count is not a property of the route: a soloist who found a low-angle, barely-fifth-class wall on the southeast side bypassing the summit cliffs downclimbed the whole thing with no rappels, and a traverse party crossed the peak without a rope. No per-station distance is published.
set.descent_text: Reverse the climbing route from the summit rather than continuing over the north ridge. Down-climb the loose, exposed class 4-5 summit ridge and ledges just south of the true summit using running belays and gear placements — this terrain is horribly loose, so treat every hold as suspect and keep the rope short between placements. At the top of the crux headwall, make one single-strand rappel down the ~10-ft near-vertical crack (roughly 5.8+ or 5.2/A1); a single 30-40m rope reaches the ledge below. Continue down and along the loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles to a rock horn draped with old rappel slings (do not trust weathered fixed tat — back it up with your own cord); from this horn, the one recorded descent made a long and a short rappel to reach an exit ledge above the couloir. One 60 m rope reaches only about 30 m per rappel and no intermediate station is known, so downclimbing may be needed there. From the exit ledge, down-climb the 40-45° northwest snow couloir, placing snow pickets or flukes as protection if conditions are firm or icy, back to the saddle just north of the peak and down to camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From camp, reverse the full glaciated approach (Challenger Glacier, West Challenger Notch, Perfect Pass, Whatcom Glacier traverse, Whatcom Pass, Brush Creek Trail, Chilliwack River Trail and cable car, Hannegan Pass) back to the Hannegan Trailhead. All anchors encountered are natural/fixed-sling (horn or gear) — there is no bolted rappel line on this route. This is not fixed: a soloist who found a low-angle, barely-fifth-class wall on the southeast side bypassing the summit cliffs downclimbed the whole route with no rappels at all, and a traverse party crossed the peak without a rope.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappelled on a single strand; a 30-40 m rope reaches the ledge below. Climbed on the ascent, this same step went at about 5.8+ free, or 5.2 with a point of aid. A distinctive cannonhole chockstone in the boulder band just above is a landmark, though it was plugged with snow when last recorded.
rappel_detail.hazards: The three other crossings do not go — the ridge-crest line would need several hundred feet of traversing out on the sheer east face. The ledges below are very exposed and covered in sand and pebbles, so footing is insecure, and the summit ridge and ledges above are loose enough that running belays and rock protection were used to downclimb them.
rappel_detail.station: At the top of the headwall that bars the upper west face, immediately beyond the band of giant boulders. The headwall runs from the ridge crest down to a lower cliff band and forms a near-impasse; the crossing is the roughly 10-ft vertical crack, the third of four lines evaluated across it — the ridge crest, a high catwalk ledge, this crack, and the bottom nose. Reached on the way down after downclimbing the summit ridge and the loose ledges below it.

review.single_rope: Searches found no single-rope descent for this peak. Only the headwall rappel is known to suit one strand of a short rope; the horn rappels were described as long and short and no intermediate station is known.
review.changed: Removed the doubled-rope setup for the horn rappels, dropped stations 2 and 3 from the table (their only content was the knotted-rope setup), and stated plainly that no single-rope line is documented there.
